rows.description: delivered_at one millisecond before the Unix epoch; negative epoch values are the classic migration trap.
placed_at exactly 1969-12-31T00:00:00Z, with updated_at at the epoch itself.
placed_at at the last millisecond of year 9999 — the maximum representable date the app can produce.
signup_date at 0001-01-01T00:00:00Z, the minimum date BSON can hold.
signup_date one millisecond after the minimum date, so millisecond precision must survive at the extreme.
updated_at carrying a non-zero millisecond component (.123).
updated_at on an exact second (milliseconds .000), the counterpart to the .123 case.
cart expires_at at year 9999 — carts that never expire are routinely stamped with a sentinel far-future date.
placed_at stored as an ISO-8601 string instead of a Date, a decade of schema drift in one field.
updated_at in a legacy US locale format, unparseable by ISO parsers.
signup_date as an ISO string with an explicit offset and a leap day.
placed_at a real Date while delivered_at for the same order is an ISO string — one document, two representations.
int32 maximum and minimum stored exactly at the boundary.
int64 maximum and minimum on money-ish fields.
int64 value past 2^53, where doubles lose integer precision.
Negative zero next to positive zero.
NaN in an aggregate field.
Positive infinity on a normally integral field.
Negative infinity in money data.
Decimal128 money value with two decimal places.
Decimal128 with 30 significant digits.
subtotal stored as int32.
subtotal stored as double in a sibling document.
Loyalty counter that outgrew int32 and is now int64.
Customer name with accented Latin, an emoji carrying a variation selector (U+FE0F), and CJK text.
Customer name stored in decomposed (NFD) form: 'Jose' + U+0301 COMBINING ACUTE ACCENT, not the precomposed 'José'.
Email stored with mixed case, as typed at signup 10 years ago.
The same logical customer email stored lowercased — a second document accumulated over the years.
Order where the coupon field exists but is the empty string.
Product description at roughly 760 characters, the kind of text that grows unbounded in a 10-year-old catalogue.
Customer name containing an apostrophe, embedded double quotes and a literal backslash next to an emoji.
Order where coupon_code is explicitly null.
Order from before the coupon feature existed: coupon_code is not present at all.
Order whose items array is present but empty.
Order with an empty history object rather than an empty array.
Product whose tags array contains a null element alongside a normal string.
An order whose history array is present but empty. Engines that treat an empty array as null, or that drop empty arrays, lose this document from a $size/$eq [] query.
History entries stored as arrays of arrays (a 10-year-old system that once used positional tuples). Index paths into nested arrays behave differently across engines.
A legacy product whose tags array accumulated strings, numbers, booleans, ObjectIds and embedded objects over ten years of schema drift.
An order where status was written as a one-element array by an old code path. A scalar equality filter must still match it.

rows.category: arrays: single object instead of array
rows.description: An order from the pre-array era where items is one embedded object, not an array of line items. The dotted path still has to resolve.
A refund history entry nested six levels deep: history[].event.meta.actor.roles and history[].event.meta.channel.region.
An embedded history entry whose keys are stored in a different order than the equality filter lists them. BSON document equality is order-sensitive at the byte level but not semantically.

rows.category: other BSON types: ObjectId, plus top-level key order
rows.description: An order keyed to a warehouse by ObjectId, with top-level fields stored in an order nothing like the filter's.
A product thumbnail stored as BSON binary subtype 00 (generic), the shape a decade of GridFS-free image blobs produces.
A customer session identifier stored as a 16-byte UUID in binary subtype 04.
A product whose active flag was written as the integer 1 by an old admin import, while the rest of the collection stores true.
